This study re-examines the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H₂ equation through a correspondence involving linear relationships to $S^{(1)}$ and $S^{(2)}$-invariant matrices. We analyze the integrability of this system by applying the $S^{(2)}$-invariant matrix Lax method, with results indicating that the matrix form of the integrable H₂ equation introduces a distinct variant capable of supporting a Bäcklund transformation.

Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) focuses on identifying interactions between objects within an image. While existing studies have primarily sought to enhance the overall detection pipeline's accuracy, such strategies often fail to address specific sub-tasks, sometimes even increasing false positives. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach called Global Context Guided Relationship Detection (GCRD), designed to mitigate false positives by incorporating global image context into local object pair analyses. Building upon the widely used pairwise modeling framework established in VPEN, our method enhances each object pair with rich image context to yield more precise predictions on bounding boxes, relationship types, and logical subject-object ordering. Context is integrated into a two-dimensional convolutional layer to extract the features; furthermore, we implement a dynamic mechanism to weigh the relevance of each object pair based on its surrounding environment. This process enables our model to identify visual properties inherent in the image sequence that signal the improbability of certain relationships, effectively filtering out false positives. Extensive experiments on the 7WEC and ReLATE datasets confirm that the proposed GCRD method significantly reduces false errors, outperforming current state-of-the-art techniques specifically regarding false positive rates.

A metric representing the residual quantum correlations between two qubits is proposed. Using this metric, the strength of quantum correlations affected by weak measurements was examined. The analysis demonstrates that weak measurements progressively decrease both entanglement and residual quantum correlations; notably, even when weak measurements are applied solely to one of the two interacting qubits, the corresponding correlations involving the other qubit decline. The relationship between this measured correlation strength and the cost of the weak measurement operation is also clarified.

Social relationships are vital across various domains, including security check, image indexing, and society. While previous research has largely depended on manual tagging to reveal these structures, this work presents the initial fully automated, machine learning approach utilizing fully connected neural networks. Specifically, it addresses two tasks: predicting co-occurrence between individuals and defining boundary boxes for those individuals. To achieve this, we suggest an encoder-endoder-decoder architecture designed to construct a social relationship graph directly from the input. The study evaluates the methodology using the newly created MMSocial dataset for task assessment purposes.

While recent advancements have established graph convolutional networks (GCNs) as a dominant force in vision recognition, they rely heavily on static, fully connected structures that fail to model the highly variable and irregular patterns inherent in graph-based visual data. This limitation motivates our investigation into learning generic, dynamic graph structures directly from data. We present an end-to-end trainable framework designed to predict graph topologies for messages passing, designed to capture local shape configurations in point clouds and object part relationships in scene graphs. Our proposed model introduces dynamic edge and node mechanisms into the standard GCN architecture; unlike prior methods that require manual design or fixed structures, this approach auto-generates complete graph topologies entirely from input features. We validate the efficacy of this dynamic structure prediction through rigorous experiments on two primary visual recognition tasks: semi-supervised classification of colored 3D shapes and graph-in- graph (GInG) classification for complex 3D object parsing. Empirical results demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms both conventional GCNs and previous approaches for dynamic graph topologies (specifically those limited to sparse graph structures) when tasked with graph classification in variable environments.

Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) is essential for numerous applications involving floating-point operations. Existing methods for MCM typically decompose constants into co-factors using the Extended Euclidean algorithm, then implement multiplications through a combination of additions, shifts, and accumulations. However, current literature offers limited guidance on achieving minimal implementation cost. This study introduces a novel MCM design methodology that significantly lowers hardware complexity by utilizing a uniform structure, which contrasts with current techniques that rely on varying designs for different multipliers. Experimental results indicate that the proposed approach reduces hardware cost by up to 20% compared to state-of-the-art MCM implementations.

Quantum deep learning integrates quantum computing methods with deep learning to explore the benefits introduced by quantum resources. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the field, outlining fundamental concepts, the evolution history, quantum-specific advantages, application areas, and the significant challenges encountered in quantum deep learning. Given the nascent and rapidly developing nature of these research efforts, numerous difficulties remain that present barriers to the future successful deployment of quantum deep learning systems.

Radio frequency (RF) acceleration technology has been instrumental in enabling contemporary high-energy physics particle colliders to reach their designed beam energies by addressing chemical ionization limitations that restrict beam lengths to mere meters. Because current and future proposed systems—including the High-Luminosity LHC, Project X, and the proposed CLIC accelerator—cannot survive beam distances exceeding kilometer scales using conventional methods, they depend entirely on RF systems for full energization. This paper presents a comprehensive review of current RF accelerator technology development efforts, identifies critical research needs for upcoming facilities, and aligns these requirements with proposed research plans and existing funding mechanisms. Specifically, it addresses the three primary acceleration methods in use today—superconducting and normal-conducting radio-frequency systems, along with beam-driven concepts—along with emerging drivers and cooling paradigms. We conclude that superconducting technologies hold the most immediate promise for achieving the necessary beam parameters for both SHiP and the Compact Linear Collider (CLIC). Furthermore, to meet the specific needs of the high-luminosity Large Hadron Collider (LHC), R&D efforts should prioritize advancements across three key areas: (1) high-power amplifiers capable of delivering 500 MW peak power with high peak-to-average ratios; (2) novel beam and structure designs that minimize electromagnetic (EM) fields to reduce beam scattering and gas desorption; and (3) cutting-edge cryogenic architectures featuring direct helium-cooled support structures and advanced thermal management systems.

Physicians and researchers have long envisioned a muon collider as a critical component of a future lepton machine. Despite this potential, the concept faces substantial design complexities stemming from the inherent properties of muons. This presentation offers an overview of the collider's conceptual framework and current status, emphasizing the significant engineering hurdles that must be overcome to realize these engineering feats.

We analyze the dispersion relations of linearized perturbations—specifically scalar, vector, and tensor modes—within a viscous relativistic fluid governed by a generalized hydrodynamic framework. This framework permits transport coefficients to vary with the variation scale and allows for coefficients not compliant with causal or stability constraints, provided they lead to stable dispersion relations. Our findings reveal a single tensor mode experiencing viscous damping, a single vector mode exhibiting amplification, and three scalar modes, the majority of which are undamped. While amplifying modes possess potential risks for fluid stability, the specific magnitude of transport coefficients and initial fluid conditions dictate whether actual instability ensues.

This study calculates the isotropic background background of Hawking radiation from primordial black holes (PBHs), specifically for photons with energies exceeding 10 eV. Due to the blackbody nature of Hawking radiation, the spectral distribution for high-energy photons declines exponentially, rendering such emission negligible unless the black hole temperature surpasses 100 eV, corresponding to a mass below $10^{-17}$ kg. Given this threshold, Hawking photon radiation in the high-energy regime originates exclusively from evaporating PBHs. We determine the spectral energy distribution of the cosmic background due to Hawking radiation from evaporating PBHs through two primary avenues: direct emission and secondary gamma rays produced by charged particle cascades. While direct emission from neutral photons constitutes only a minor fraction, the total background is overwhelmingly shaped by charged particle cascades. We further examine the constraints these backgrounds impose on the abundance of evaporating PBHs. While existing observational data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory, the Hubble Space Telescope's Near-Infrared Instrument, and the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Mission provide some limits, they do not fully cover the entire mass spectrum of PBHs. We propose that the Inverse Comember Process Instrumentation on the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope provides more stringent constraints for PBHs with masses between $10^{-15}$ and $10^{-14}$ grams. Additionally, we argue that the spectral energy distribution of the cosmological background offers significant

We introduce Virtual Secure Platform (VSP), the inaugural general-purpose secure multi-party computation (SMPC) processor virtual machine built upon a formal specification. To enable efficient computation, our design leverages Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) over negacyclic rings, specifically the TFHE scheme, allowing operations on encrypted data with only latency overheads for basic arithmetic and logical operations. We adapted the x86-64 architecture for VSP and developed a custom pipeline featuring five specialized stages: Fetch, Decode, Execute, Memory, and Writeback. To demonstrate the processor's versatility, we provide 19 formal specifications covering diverse functions, including control flow management.

Valued Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs) involve assigning labels from generic valued domains to variables to maximize the total weight of satisfied binary relations. While finding an optimal solution is generally NP-hard within these non-Boolean valued frameworks (unlike in standard Boolean cases where they are complete for NP), identifying a near-optimal one can be achieved in polynomial time through specific structural properties. This capability manifests as either an exact fixing or a parameterized approximation scheme (PTAS) or PSOS. This paper establishes the former or latter for sparse valued CSPs, focusing on problems with sparse instance graphs that exhibit either bounded treewidth or a bounded number of bounded-size constraints, or those exhibiting bounded fractional edge-covariance.

Pre-trained language models have achieved significant success across numerous Natural Language Processing tasks. However, they require substantial computational resources and storage, as they necessitate heavy model loading and, in many cases, per-batch inference for processing. Current parsing approaches based on these models are inefficient, conducting inductive head and dependency depth calculations after language model scores are processed. This inefficiency is addressed by introducing a novel parsing method that operates directly using attention weights from the pre-trained model without post-hoc processing. This approach eliminates the need for additional parameters or post-training, maintaining the integrity of the original model. Experimental results using BERT demonstrate parsing performance that is comparable to state-of-the-art methods on development and test sets in few-shot scenarios for CoNLL 2018 and 2012 (and 2012-2020), as well as in zero-shot scenarios for CoNLL 2020. Furthermore, our method reduces the inductive overhead associated with pre-trained models by approximately two orders of magnitude.

High-resolution Hyperspectral Images (HSIs) capture spectral signatures across numerous bands, providing rich material-level details that are ideal for fine-grained analysis. However, their large volume creates substantial storage and computational burdens. This study leverages HSIs to enhance semantic segmentation for urban scenes, utilizing their spectral nuance to substitute traditional reliance on pixel-level granularity. We introduce a HSI-based weakly-supervised segmentation framework that creates semantic labels by locally fusing adjacent HSI segments, thereby increasing reliance between neighboring pixels to mitigate the high computational load. A novel uncertainty-aware attention mechanism is integrated to selectively amplify informative regions while suppressing noise. Furthermore, we derive a surrogate function to facilitate optimization, ensuring global consistency within the segmentation process. Extensive validation across three distinct datasets confirms the method's superior performance and robustness.

Recent observations by the TESS mission have identified a growing number of hot, synchronous sub-surface giants displaying anomalous, rapid spin rates on their surfaces. We investigate whether these stars could be the result of planetary engulfment, a phenomenon predicted to produce rapid rotation due to the transfer of a planet's angular momentum into the stellar interior. We demonstrate that engulflement yields a generic signature: a negative correlation between surface rotation period and the fraction of envelope consumed. This occurs because less momentum input leads to shorter (faster) spin times, resulting in the observation of ingressed events at millisecond-scale periods for TESS's sensitive detection thresholds. We further show that most such events would currently remain undetected due to short observation durations, as they require ingestion times exceeding current typical limits to reveal this correlation. Additionally, we argue this correlation offers a robust diagnostic for distinguishing genuine engulflement events from potential false positives. Finally, we suggest that if no such correlation is found, it would imply that even in scenarios where planets penetrate deeply, extremely efficient angular momentum transport rapidly moves that momentum further inward, preventing it from significantly altering stellar spin rates.

Session-based recommendations rely on capturing user behaviors to achieve real-time, high-efficiency tracking. While graph neural networks (GNNs) are widely employed for this task, they often suffer from oversmoothness and insufficient induction of graph structure. This study introduces a graph co-training framework utilizing self-supervised learning to address these inherent limitations. Specifically, we generate self-supervised views of graph data by strategically masking and reordering node features and adjacency matrices. Our proposed model, SGCT (Session-based Graph Co-training), divides GNN encoders into two distinct networks to achieve robust generalization across them, incorporating an session-embedding co-training mechanism to effectively merge sequential context with item representations. Experiments conducted on three major session-based datasets demonstrate that SGCT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art recommendation algorithms.

This paper introduces the concepts of group LCD and group reversible LCD linear codes. We establish that every cyclic code, as well as every quasi-cyclic code of length $lm$ where $l$ is any positive integer and $l$ is prime, qualifies as a group LCD code. Furthermore, we derive lower and upper bounds for the dimensions of group LCD codes. Specific examples include providing examples of new, high-dimensional group LCD codes, as well as the shortest such codes, based on the Grassl and Nebe tables for distances up to $d\leq 9$.

Although recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are recognized for their exceptional object categorization and visual scene memory capabilities, the underlying mechanisms of their long-term recurrent representations remain unclear. To address this, we examined trained object categorization RNNs, revealing that their recurrent states predominantly consist of diverse, temporal dynamics object features which largely respect hierarchical organization from lower to higher levels within the visual hierarchy. Additionally, a single dimension of recurrent dynamics effectively captures features spanning the entire object categorization hierarchy, with (1) gradient descent efficiently positioning these dimensions to isolate specific categorical information and (2) manual intervention successfully replacing standard dimensions with individual neuron activations to boost categorization performance. These findings indicate that RNNs utilize dynamically structured, hierarchical object features for visualization and suggest that recurrent layers function as efficient generators of precise, sparse explanations for decision-making during tasks.

A key feature of non-Hermitian topological phases is point-gap topology, which disappears under an ergodic phase transition into a fully correlated random state. This study reveals another mechanism, specifically in correlated non-Hhertigan 1D models, that can partially reduce point-gap topology. We analyze an interacting extension of the non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, defined by asymmetric hopping and gain-loss potentials, across both interacting and non-interacting regimes. Using star graph diagrams, we derive exact conditions for non-Hermitian band structures with or without point gaps. Furthermore, by applying the star graph framework alongside the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) method, we demonstrate a smooth transition from a topological state characterized by unit winding numbers to a fully correlated random state where these point gaps are entirely eliminated. Finally, we identify an intermediate region of non-trivial topology where the winding numbers are fractional, filling the topological properties between the fully trivial and totally disconnected limits.

Despite this advantage, realizing such high efficacy with Golay results is challenging. This paper presents novel construction techniques for multistage GCAs in configurations of two and three dimensions, specifically targeting GCAs with phase values of $\pm 1$ or $\pm 1 \pm j$. First, we introduce general frameworks for generating GCAs with arbitrary length $L$ using specific unitary DFT matrix sets. Detecting binary changes between co-registered hyperspectral images is crucial for monitoring the environment and military applications. Current methods are either too computationally demanding or fail to effectively utilize limited data. To address these challenges, this paper introduces an unsupervised deep learning approach for binary change detection in hyperspectral datasets. This technique integrates feature fusion deep convolutional autoencoders, which merge information from two distinct autoencders. Empirical validation on three datasets—the Gobi, GaoKang, and RSC P4D—demonstrates that the proposed technique significantly improves detection accuracy, as evidenced by superior performance in AUC and F1 scores compared to existing state-of-the-art benchmarks.

This study presents a first-ever experiment measuring the range of spin-exchange interactions between individual atoms in silicon. Conducting operations within an electron double quantum dot system situated in a magnetic field, we perform precise electron injections across a broad spectrum of translational valley states and two distinct energy ranges. By monitoring the influence of these factors on the local dwell time fluctuation, we track the decay processes. Our results reveal that the calculated mean free paths for spin-exchange in silicon are approximately two to three orders of magnitude smaller than current theoretical predictions. These observations provide direct experimental evidence, supplementing previous theorems, concerning silicon's nanoscale spin-exchange dynamics.

Optimization methods are increasingly vital across numerous scientific and commercial domains, yet developing effective solutions remains a persistent challenge. To support the rapid development and testing of novel algorithms, researchers currently rely on a collection of scattered, obscure, and incomplete software libraries. This paper introduces **LibOPT**, an open-source framework dedicated to accelerating the initial prototyping phase of optmization techniques. By integrating established libraries for specific tasks—such as generating test functions, solving problems, and performing scenario analysis—this tool enables quick implementation using cutting-edge methodologies. Additionally, the paper offers a comprehensive evaluation of this software during early stages of development and proposes a streamlined development workflow, illustrated through a working case study of a method designed for a variant of the Traveling Salesperson Problem.

Let $G$ be a reductive group defined over a local field $F$, and consider its action on an algebraic variety $X$. We define the multiplicity $t(X,G)$ as the largest integer $n$ for which there exist $n+1$ elements within $G$ that are simultaneously regular for every pair of functions in an open subset of an irreducible closed subset of an invariant subspace of $X$, where this subset has dimension maximized within the general fiber of the function field of $X$. This paper establishes several properties regarding this multiplicity and introduces a specific homogeneous algebraic variety concept to demonstrate that $\forall n \geq 1$, there exists a variety $X_n$ such that $t(X_n,G) = n$. Furthermore, it proves that for any variety $X$, there exists a reductive subgroup $G'$ of $G$ such that $X$ is $G'$-homogeneous if and only if there exists a $G'$-homogeneous variety $Y$ with $t(Y,G') \leq t(X,G)$. Examples provided in this work include algebraic groups, homogeneous spaces, and unipotent varieties.

We question the validity of applying second quantization within non-commutative quantum field theories (NCQFTs) due to significant difficulties. While it is possible to construct an NCQFT using second quantization on a Hilbert space that exhibits non-commutative anti-commutation or anti-symmetric relations, this construction does not constitute an NCQFT in the standard, widely accepted definition. The root of the problem lies in the incompatibility between non-local non-commutative coordinates and the specific quantum statistics—whether fermionic or bosonic—underpinning such field theories.

We introduce a two-photon absorption edge transient-current method designed for visualizing and quantifying charge transport within wide-bandgap materials. Using synthetic, single-crystalline diamond slabs treated with UV illumination across the UV-A/UV-B spectrum, we generated and tracked the movement of electron-hole pairs through transient photocurrents. By systematically varying the excitation wavelength, we obtained three-dimensional maps of the resulting current to scrutinize charge dynamics across the diamond bandgap. These findings, benchmarked against time-of-flight measurements, align well with previous reports on carrier lifetime and mobility. Furthermore, these maps reveal that charge transport efficiency is not uniform throughout the diamond spectrum; instead, it peaks when UV-B light excites carriers near the valence-band edge. We anticipate this technique will facilitate broader investigations into the electronic properties of other robust insulators.

The rise of toxic content on social media platforms—including hate speech, offensive language, and misogyny—has prompted extensive academic investigation into detection methodologies. While much existing work focuses on English texts, there is a critical lack of research and developed tools addressing Arabic toxic content. To address this gap, we introduce a novel multi-task deep learning architecture designed to identify these forms of toxicity within the Arabic context. Our system performs two simultaneous tasks: classifying individual sentences containing abusive language and identifying the specific category of abuse per sentence. We evaluate the model's performance against both standalone classifiers and naive multi-task baselines. Additionally, we analyze the impact of shared representation layers on model capabilities and examine feature representations through the lens of visualizing the final layer's output space.

This paper explores the solvability of specific fractional backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs) characterized by a delayed drift function and inhomogeneous components within that drift. This study focuses on BSDEs linked to a fractional operator in the generator, situated between two classical cases: standard backward stochastic differential equations and those associated with扑热风 (Pontryagin) problems. By applying an iterative technique, we establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions for this category of equations. Furthermore, we derive a convergence result for the generator's approximation and set forth to find an analytical solution to a particular application-based illustration.

Model-based reinforcement learning aims to approximate an optimal policy by learning a world model that estimates the true environment, often yielding superior sample efficiency compared to model-free approaches. This study investigates the robustness and generalization capabilities of policies developed through this framework under slight environmental shifts. We introduce a new probabilistic policy search algorithm tailored for world-model-based method learning, demonstrating through simulation that this strategy produces highly robust and generalizing policies capable of withishing minor, random perturbations.

In a network environment where the source has limited transmission bandwidth $R$ bandwidth limitations, it becomes necessary to store data at the receivers with limited storage capacity, $M$. The objective is to store as much information as possible at the network's endpoints, given $N$ total files and $N$ users, while ensuring that every user can recover all $N$ files with a per-user rate no greater than $R$. This task is essentially equivalent to the problem of index coding. This work introduces a method to model coded caching and distributed computation schemes using a tripartite graph. We establish that the maximum amount of information that can be stored at the network's endpoints, $M$, is equal to the minimum size of an optimal vertex cover in this graph. This result provides a way to prove the optimality of existing coded caching and distributed computing methods. This approach is also extensible to scenarios involving non-uniform file lengths and receivers with differing storage capacities.

We construct the univalent type-theoretic counterpart to Plotkin's game semantemics for PCO in univalent type theory, extending the work initiated by Shao. Building directly on results from Shao and Yoneya, we demonstrate that the univalent type-theoretic version of PCO has an equivalent relationship to the UType model of Dreyer and others. Additionally, we introduce a novel perspective on the connection between PCO's stable functions and the weaker continuity condition required within homotopy type theory.

This paper examines the pole cancellation behavior of automorphic Eisenstein series for $GL(n, \mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ at the trivial character and its dual within the irreducible induced representation derived from a Hecke character of a narrow congruence subgroup defined over $\mathbb{Q}$. These findings generalize recent research by the second and third authors regarding cases for $GL(n+1, \mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ and $GL(n, \mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ respectively, extending it here to an arbitrary reductive group over $\mathbb{Q}$ of either type.

Addressing collision avoidance is a central challenge in robotics. While theoretical frameworks like Control Barrier Functions (CBF) exist, existing CBF-based safety controllers often fail to account for mobile platform dynamics, resulting in high-frequency, destabilizing low-and-order oscillations known as "chattering." This issue is particularly evident when robotic arms operate at the edge of safety barriers. This work introduces a new Saturated CBF (S-CBF) controller that is motion-aware and integrated within a model predictive framework to ensure safe tracking for mobile humanoid robots. By incorporating the specific characteristics of dynamic motion into the design, the proposed controller significantly mitigates chattering caused by abrupt control switches. Simulation results featuring a bipedal platform demonstrate that the motion-aware CBF controller offers superior stability compared to both the traditional, non-motion-aware CBF approach and baseline motion dynamics ignoring methods.

Natural language processing is a critical academic area focused on comprehending digital text, a process frequently hindered by inadequate digital representations arising from the wide variety of human speech patterns. This paper proposes a solution by applying graph theory to exact extractive sentence selection, ultimately forming a compressed text output. The proposed methodology employs graphs to model the relationships between sentences, employing established graph algorithms to identify the most significant sentences. These sentences are then exactly extracted to create the final summary.

We examine the Eckhaus and Josephson instabilities within a BEC subjected to a nonlinear $\pi$-beam splitter, revealing that while nonlinearities amplify an Eckhaus instability, the BEC density remains stable against Josephaneous transitions due to $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry preservation. Conversely, we utilize a nonlinear beam splitter to engineer custom, tailored nonlinear transformations—referred to as quantum gates—for the system's components.

This work explores the unicity of meromorphic maps $f$ senting a complete K\"{a}hler manifold into a projective variety. Building on recent findings by the second author regarding the unicity of generalized holomorphic maps in projective space, we extend these concepts to the case of $f$ mapping into a projective variety, establishing several new results. Key improvements over the first author's findings by the second author (and their generalization to projective varieties) are demonstrated. Key results include:

The resolution of nonlinear geometric phenomena often relies on solving systems of polynomials, which may yield solutions with unexpected dimensions due to the inclusion of the nondegenerate locus within a singular hull. Isolating this nondegenerate locus holds particular value in applications like computer graphics and virtual reality, where it corresponds to a less constrained subsystem that captures the core geometric structure. This paper introduces a signature-based algorithm to compute the nondegenerate locus efficiently.

Spatial anti-aliasing is critical for both the visual quality and rendering performance of line joins where segments meet on 2D vector maps. Existing solutions often fail to provide efficient anti-aliasing for these specific map joins. This paper introduces a method that applies efficient spatial anti-aliasing specifically to map joins. The approach precalculates blending information using a specialized data structure designed to support rapid query operations. This precomputation enables the rendering engine to calculate precise alpha values for pixel coverage quickly during execution. This stage involves calculating the overlap between a defined screen-area bounding box and feature geometry, utilizing an $O(\log n)$ time algorithm. Furthermore, a experimental assessment was conducted to compare this technique against a baseline method relying on simple geometric formulas for area calculation.

Multiquadric quasi-interpolation via univariate function scaling fails to preserve local minimum preservation due to its non-monotonicity. By applying the positive part operation to the multiquadric through the function $f(x) = \frac{1}{2}(|x|+x+1)$, a new quasi-interpolation scheme is developed using the resulting quasi-concave function. This method exceeds multiquadric in accuracy and maintains local minima. The analysis demonstrates that this method produces a shape preserving, stable approximation that converges to the target function.

Pulsar halos, defined as a newly identified class of extended gamma-ray emitting structures surrounding pulsars, result from radiation produced by relativistic electrons and positrons within these regions. This review examines the observational data, theoretical models, and specific pulsar sources associated with pulsar halos within our Galaxy. Observations primarily rely on data from the Fermi-LAT mission, which has detected electron-positron emission around several young neutron star remnants. Since such emission serves as a definitive indicator of a particle accelerator at the pulsar site, pulsar halos provide crucial insights into the propagation of relativistic antimatter electrons and positrons in the Galaxy. We present a catalog of pulsar candidates that could exhibit halo emission. Furthermore, we analyze two prominent examples—Pulsar Wind Nebulae (PWN) associated with the Crab Nebula and the supernova remnant PWN G106.3+2.6—to discuss pulsar halo formation mechanisms. Our discussion also covers emission characteristics from the nearby Crab supernova remnant, specifically its surrounding halo, as well as distinct features of positron annihilation lines observed near the Vela pulsar. We conclude by outlining prospects for detecting additional pulsar halos using the CTA observatory.

Adverse weather conditions frequently disrupt transportation networks, causing significant economic losses. To effectively mitigate these impacts during extreme events, it is essential to implement efficient detection and classification systems. Currently, automated methods often fail due to the limited generalizability of their trained models when deployed in real-world settings. Additionally, the paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of various CNN architectures for image classification tasks. Experimental results indicate that our newly proposed augmentation method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, while the evaluated CNNs provide robust baselines for future research.

Soft grippers are increasingly valued for grasping delicate and fragile objects due to their compliance. However, their non-linear dynamics, significant softness, and high sensitivity to contact forces create difficulties for both modeling and control. This study introduces an online modeling and low-latency control strategy for multi-fingered soft grippers, achieving precise control despite nonlinear behaviors, nonlinear sensing, and external disturbances. By employing the spectral decomposition of the discrete-time dynamical system, we construct a global linear approximation using the spectral variables of each gripper finger. Furthermore, we develop an iterative control scheme that integrates this linear approximation with an explicitly designed error correction term to ensure convergence to the original nonlinear manifold. To guarantee stable behavior, the magnitude of spectral variables is constrained, allowing for stable, explicit closed-form solutions for control inputs. This approach yields an iterative, model-based control algorithm that provides stable, large-scale motion control with guaranteed steady-state accuracy. Experimental validation demonstrates the system's robustness against nonlinear dynamics, nonlinear measurement processes, and sensor noise.

Optimization challenges are central to theoretical computer science, with significant strides made over the past few decades, particularly within Machine Learning contexts involving high-dimensional gradient descent. This line of research encompasses concepts such as smoothness, strong convexity, eigenvalue gaps, and average curvature, which guide how initial problem parameters influence final outcomes. While much effort addressed discrete optimization, this work extends gradient descent principles continuously to the natural gradient descent framework. By examining key geometric and spectral properties, we demonstrate optimality conditions for both gradient descent and natural gradient descent across both Euclidean and Riemannian settings. Consequently, these findings suggest a broader framework for generalizing other optimizational algorithms.

This study introduces a multimodal deep learning framework designed to predict outcomes in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Utilizing data from 109 NSCLC patients sourced from the IMCLUNG dataset, the research combines histopathological images and radiological CT images. First, the histopathological features are extracted through the Fine-Grained Whole Slide Image (FG-WSI) module, while radiological features are derived from a 3D Convolutional Neural Network applied to CT scans. Next, these complementary representations are fused via summation within a fully connected layer, followed by classification to predict patient outcomes. Evaluated using the FG-WSI and CT modalities separately as well as in combination, this model achieved 70.8%, 71.4%, and improvement in survival prediction accuracy, respectively. Consequently, these findings confirm that integrating histopathological and radiological data significantly enhances prognostic performance.

Representing states is crucial for learning processes and agents in Reinforcement Learning. In many practical scenarios, state information is delivered through natural language, such as visual question answering in natural language or dialogue in tasks. This paper reviews methods for creating natural language state representations for deep reinforcement learning. We begin by defining different types of natural language representation for state in this domain. Next, we examine approaches that utilize pre-trained models to create these representations, such as word embeddings, phrase vectors, and contextual vector spaces. We also discuss techniques for training from the ground up using various architectural frameworks. Finally, we conclude by assessing current achievements in this field and pointing out directions for future research.

We introduce a machine learning methodology designed to recover the power density spectrum (PDS) of the universe from individual quasar spectra. Our framework employs a U-Net convolutional neural network, initially trained on synthetic spectra-generated by the radiative transfer code "Cosmo4QSO." This initial training enables the model to accurately predict the PDS from observed spectral data across the redshift range $0.5 < z < 3.5$. Beyond the initial phase, our system remains robust against specific quirks inherent in real observational datasets, correctly identifying and modeling the expected PDS despite the presence of cosmic voids and an overabundance of Lyman-$\alpha$ absorption lines. Furthermore, we apply the model to extract power spectrum components corresponding to distinct mass scales, demonstrating that even with these minimal assumptions, the recovered features align closely with predictions from standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmology.

Gravitational wave memory refers to a permanent displacement in proper distances between free-falling test masses resulting from passing gravitational waves. Although this effect is absent in linearized gravity, it emerges as a leading-order contribution to the post-linear order of gravitational radiation. Because different polarization components of the memory vanish on average, any generation of memory on cosmological scales would produce a distinct stochastic background, detectable by both ground-based detectors and pulsar timing arrays, with a unique signature that sets it apart from standard stochastic sources.

Supersymmetry (SUSY) offers a theoretically motivated framework for SUSY-breaking that could account for both the observed scale of axion signatures and the generation of primordial gravitational waves via first-order phase transitions. We present here a model where such a transition occurs within the hidden sector and naturally generates PeV-scale gravitinos during the transition itself, with the model's parameters determined by Grand Unified Theory (GUT) considerations. The gravitational signal from the first-order transition occurs in the high-frequency domain ($f \sim 10$ Hz) and is potentially accessible to future pulsar timing array observations, while the model also generates a population of primordial black holes through gravitational wave generation.

In this scenario, the mechanism of baryon number creation (leptogenesis) operates via the decays of these gravitinos, with the specific branching ratios on the baryon versus lepton number dictated by the SUSY-breaking mechanism. We analyze a specific instance of this model to demonstrate its viability.

Semantic communication aims to enhance the efficiency of wireless links by conveying the essential meanings of source data rather than raw signals. This paper introduces an innovative Emergent Semantic Communication (ESC) framework that ensures reliable communication through the collaborative learning of semantic representations and symbols during adverse channel conditions. This framework integrates neural and symbolic causal reasoning with signaling theory to facilitate efficient and robust data transmission. Specifically, a neuro-symbolic causal reasoning (NSCR) architecture is utilized to extract high-level semantic features and generate semantic symbols from received signals, while an evolutionary signaling game is employed to train a transmitter encoding scheme capable of generating corresponding semantic symbols. This synergistic approach enables both receiver and sender to jointly develop consistent semantic symbols and symbols generation mechanisms via the transmitter, resulting in a stable equilibrium that stabilizes communication performance. Numerical evaluations confirm that this proposed ESC framework achieves superior performance compared to conventional methods, delivering higher reliability and efficiency benefits.

Recent progress in Session-based Recommendation (SB-Rec) relies heavily on neural architectures that encode each item based on its immediate predecessor within a specific session. This paper introduces a SNN-based, two-stage model designed to capture both long-term and short-term item dependencies effectively. In an initial stage, the approach generates global stage-level Candidate Rank Embeddings (CREs) for every item by aggregating individual embeddings from the final output of a short-term auto-encoder specific to that session's long history. Subsequently, these aggregated CREs are utilized in a second stage to predict whether an item appears in a given session. Experimental results on three widely-used datasets confirm that the proposed framework significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art SB-rec models. Furthermore, CREs demonstrate their ability to isolate and represent distinct long-term patterns, establishing them as a potent tool for enhancing recommendation quality.

We investigate a pair of interacting active colloids moving within an activity gradient by applying a hydrodynamically mediated interaction model, which we extend to incorporate individual particle polarity and varying strength of particle-scale activity. This extension allows for an analytical treatment of the system's average behavior, which we then compare against non-interacting simulations of particles that are explicitly modeled with hydrodynamic interactions. Our results demonstrate that the macroscopic movement of the dual-particle "colloidal molecule" functions as a sensor for the environment's energy gradient; this sensory capability relies on a mismatch between the two-particle and single-particle activity levels. This phenomenon, which holds a clear biophysical implication regarding molecular ratcheting, is robustly explained by a simple analytical model of effective forces acting on the system.

We introduce a discrete fracture network (DFN) model designed to simulate fluid flow within porous media. The methodology represents the domain as a union of discrete networks and surrounding matrix blocks intersected by network planes, with all elements embedded in a three-dimensional mesh that conforms to their individual geometric boundaries. Equations governing the fracture network blocks are solved using a mimetic finite difference approach that preserves discrete conservation laws, ensuring the satisfaction of discrete differential identities. This computational strategy relies on the concept of dual mesh, where each primal element has a corresponding dual counterpart positioned at its barycenter. The study develops a dual mesh strategy to generate an adaptive mesh suitable for DFN modeling and integrates this with the solution of flow equations. Finally, the proposed framework is validated through a series of tests examining various aspects, including matrix-fracture coupling, fracture connectivity, and matrix contributions to matrix capacity.

This study addresses two critical challenges in drone swarms: collision avoidance and shape preservation during flight. It introduces two original methods, both relying on center-based point-set registration. The first approach prevents collisions by dynamically registering every pair of drones in the formation, a strategy that avoids the high computational load of traditional model-predictive control techniques while maintaining formation geometry. The second method preserves the desired formation shape by periodically realigning the entire group to its target configuration through registration. This method updates the swarm's trajectory on the fly when external disturbances occur, ensuring robustness against wind and turbulence. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed strategies effectively preserve formation geometry and successfully prevent collisions.

This study concentrates on a mean-field optimal control framework involving stochastic differential equations fueled by fractional Brownian motion (FBM), a continuous Gaussian process exhibiting long-range dependence and non-Markovian characteristics that serves as an extension of standard Brownian motion. Since FB cannot be directly integrated into stochastic control due to its non-Markov nature, we embed the original problem into an enlarged Markovian setting. By introducing an auxiliary time arrow, we construct augmented dynamics that resolve the long-memory effect, thereby enabling the derivation of a Hamiltonian and associated Maximum Principle for the optimized control. Furthermore, under specific convexity assumptions, we establish the sufficient conditions sufficient for optimality within this framework.

This work introduces a new two-parameter family of explicitly defined, finite-band, periodic potentials for a Dirac operator, where the associated $J$-self-adjoint direct sum of two Dirac operators exhibits a band-gap structure determined by four real parameters. Although these $J$-self-adjoint components themselves are not $J$-Hermitian, they fall under what can be described as "elliptic" within the context of $J$-self-adjoint operators. By setting this operator potential to zero and focusing on the resulting $J$-Hermitian combination, one obtains constant potential. Conversely, by selecting specific values for the four real parameters that define the operator without $J$-Hermitian properties, one generates a new family of non-Hermitian, elliptic, finite-band periodic potentials for a single Dirac operator. These potentials yield exactly four distinct band edges for the corresponding $J$-self-adjoint direct sum.

Knowledge distillation serves as an effective strategy for accelerating deep learning inference, yet the typical knowledge distillation process is hindered in security-sensitive scenarios by access limitations to both the trained teacher model and its weights. To overcome these barriers, this work introduces a decision-based black-box model that remains compatible with decision-based attacks, such as adversarial examples or label queries. Since direct distillation is impossible without explicit access to the outputs of the original teacher, this approach instead treats the black-box model as the student and employs a generative method to reconstruct the input outputs that would have been produced by the original teacher. This involves retraining a reversible neural network by minimizing the discrepancy between the actual outputs of the black-box model and those simulated by the student, effectively estimating the input features capable of generating specific black-box decisions. The method then uses these reconstructed inputs to retrain a black-box-specific generator, refining the estimates of what the original teacher knew based on available query data. Finally, a distilled model is created using this simulated knowledge for the original teacher, significantly outperforming standard random initialization methods. The effectiveness of this technique is validated through rigorous testing on multiple public datasets, including MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, as well as the PRID.2010 and ReID-164 datasets.

Imitation learning represents a dominant strategy for encoding human expertise into robotic control policies, yet its efficacy is constrained by the necessity for extensive expert demonstrations. To address this constraint, this paper introduces a new method that requires no such demonstrations. Instead, this approach utilizes common data accessible to the robot to simultaneously refine a generative agent and the target controller. By jointly training these components, they become synchronized, enabling the controller to emulate the implicit behaviors encoded within the agent's generated actions. evaluated through extensive tests on diverse mobile and manipulative tasks, our results demonstrate significant advancements in sample efficiency and total learning performance when compared to current state-of-the-art alternatives.

This study addresses a methodology for calculating the distance of linear codes constructed using Polynomials with a one-variable degree constraint, commonly referred to as PAC codes. We achieve this by determining the distance of associated multivariate codes and employing a framework that analyzes multivariate monomial correlations to support the proposed approach.

We introduce a novel system designed to track hands and re-enact their interactions with objects from unordered point cloud sequences captured in natural settings. Unlike most prior research that focuses on hands isolated from objects or treats both entities independently, our methodology models the interaction itself, allowing the reconstruction process to reflect specific how hands grasp and manipulate items. The system is built on a dual-level representation: a global free-form deformation (FFD) of hands derived from the ISL-20 dataset and a local FFD for objects selected from the CHOP dataset. These levels converge during an optimization phase that jointly refines hand and object poses while simultaneously locating and aligning two sets of pre-trained 3D Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) detectors within the point cloud to achieve high-precision tracking. Validation on challenging real-world sequences demonstrates that the proposed interaction-aware architecture significantly outperforms existing methods that process hands and objects separately.

These relations fully determine a finite presentation for the infinite complex through its two-dimensional two-skeleton, which we construct as an infinite graph on this specific number theory. Our work generalizes previous findings by Brink and Savin, who addressed the case with an interlacing number of one.

While existing techniques for identifying interference rely on tailored randomized experiments and conditioning-based tests centered on specific units, we provide criteria for selecting appropriate units within our proposed framework and demonstrate that traditional methods remain valid for them. Simulation results show our method outperforms existing approaches across a range of scenarios, except in specific cases of sparse neighborhoods where our technique excels.

We investigate neutrino emissions resulting from annihilation processes involving dark matter (fermionic or bosonic) mediated by pseudoscalar particles, specifically examining scenarios within the environment of neutron stars. Calculated energy distributions for these neutrinos are presented, alongside a derived constraint on the neutron star's maximum mass that depends on the pseudoscalar couplings to nucleons and dark matter. Additionally, we explore how neutrino opacities are affected by these new interactions at various stellar temperatures.

UNIONS/CFIS is a large-scale survey designed to image approximately 100 square degrees of the sky using the Small and Medium Science Instrument (SMISI) components of the Telescopio Nacional Juan Carlos I 1.04-m telescope in La Palma. It employs multi-epoch observations across visible and near-infrared wavelengths to achieve high temporal resolution within days. This paper introduces ShapePipe, a pipeline developed to streamline shape measurements for UNIONS/Byu images by automating the execution of the SExtractor and Byu software tools within a distributed environment using GridTools. We validate UNIONS/CFIS lensing capabilities through a demonstration application of the Cluster Lensing And Gravity Science Alliance (CLASs) strategy. Specifically, we assess the accuracy of our galaxy ellipticity estimates by applying them to a simulated cluster lensing map, ultimately establishing the relationship between shears and cluster mass.

Rédei establishes the equivalence, through two dimensions of diophantine equivalence, between the equitration of linear subspaces of $\mathbb{T}^d$ and the common diophantry of these subspace parallel affine hyperplanes. This work extends that theorem by introducing a new parameter, $\alpha$, which determines the speed at which the equivalence holds. Specifically, if a finite-dimensional linear subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is "2-good" with exponent $\alpha$, it signifies the equitration of the corresponding subspace of $\mathbb{T}^n$ with exponent $\alpha + 1$. Furthermore, we demonstrate the possibility of finding subspaces with exponent $\alpha$ that is strictly greater.

We demonstrate that local complete intersection $k$-rational singularities exhibit the $k$-Du Bois property, while for hypersurfaces, $k$-rationality implies $k$-Du Bois satisfaction. This result completes a parallel to the relationship between rational and Du Bois global singularities, which was established by Hara and Smith. In addition, we derive several consequences concerning the resolution of singularities over fields of positive characteristic.

We introduce a polarizable, electric-field-tunable Frenkel-Kentelrotlein-Berezinskii (Frenckel-Kenteltein) model that extends the classic 2D Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a square lattice by including local electronic degrees of freedom coupled with dipolar interactions. These interactions enable spatial control via external electric fields. Our theoretical work, supported by first-principles calculations and Monte Carlo simulations, shows that applying this tunable long-range force can significantly modify spin interactions, leading to a transition from magnetic ordering to spin liquid states characterized by power-law spin-spin correlations. Notably, these correlated states exhibit weak spin-spin coupling sufficient to induce a BEC of magnetic spinons, resembling the behavior found in 2D superconducting systems.

We investigate a dark matter framework where a subdominant axion component exists alongside the primary axion-dominated sector, and a subdominant sterile-neutrino component runs parallel to its main counterpart. This model is motivated by the mechanism generating the axion's mass being insufficient alone, thereby necessitating sterile neutrinos, and by cosmological constraints on the axion signal strength that allow this mixed composition. We analyze the impact of this specific axion-subdominant and two-tiered sterile-neutrino architecture on cosmology and astrophysical research into dark matter.

This work enhances the evidence supporting the view that magic states are inherently complex by deriving a tighter upper limit for their stabilizer rank. We demonstrate that for an $n$-qubit magic state within the T-subgroup, its stabilizer rank $\text{rank}(\text{St})$ satisfies the inequality $\text{rank}(\textSt) \geq \frac{4^n}{\text{rank}(\textSt)^2}$. Our findings significantly improve upon the bound established by Bravyi and significantly improve upon previous work by Haah and Keller.

This study applies a Tsallis holographic dark energy framework to multiblack hole systems and investigates the evolution of universe energy density and the equation of state parameter. We specifically analyze these dynamics within a plane-symmetric spacetime featuring two static black holes, examining how they vary with respect to the spatial coordinate $y$. Additionally, we explore the physical behavior of this dark energy under the complex-form quintessence model.

From January 2019 to July 2020, the LAMOST Time Domain (TD) survey was conducted using the eight 1.3-meter class 1D fiber scanning plates located in the LAMOST Complex, specifically targeting the K1 through K4 regions. Utilizing the 1D TD mode, each plate completed a three-month observing run with a cadence of approximately 10 days. Over the course of two years, the first four plates scanned a total area of 4000 deg$^2$ (1,000 deg$^2$ per plate), establishing LAMOST's fourth-largest high-cadence time-domain dataset. This study presents preliminary findings from the data collected by four specific scanning lanes. The mean magnitude range spans from 8.5 to 13 in U, g, r, and i bands, with a standard deviation of 0.95 days around the mean for variability periods. Under the influence of varying voltages, SRAM exhibits unique charge distribution patterns that result in distinct memory states upon readout, creating data diversity driven by physical imperfections. Resistive switch devices are rapidly emerging as a viable approach for achieving stable single-electron memory. To investigate this concept, we designed and simulated nanoscale devices featuring liquid phase resistance switching, where the active medium consists of a nanodroplet of polar solvent containing dissolved ions. Our study focused on the specific case of formamidinium nitrate suspended in water at the molecular nanoscale. The device architecture comprises a gold nanosphere nanoelectrode positioned near two nanopore silver electrodes. We applied a high-voltage alternating current to the central sphere to induce the formation of negative and positive colloids at opposing sides of the water droplet; once these colloids become trapped within the silver nanopores, the device function as memory states by altering their resistance. The simulation results indicate that the proposed design operates effectively at the molecular nanoscale while maintaining strong single-electron effects even when the fluid dimension reaches approximately 100 nm in diameter.

Recent advances in spectroscopy have enabled the direct observation of elementary excitations within oxide systems. Under the influence of strong electron-electron and electron-orbital-coupling interactions, electrons in transition metal oxides exhibit a complex behavior that deviates significantly from standard single-particle picture. This work provides a comprehensive overview of spectral features found in $d$-block oxide materials, interpreting them through the lens of interacting electron model calculations. We examine how electron-electron interactions drive collective excitations in spin and orbital sectors, while also addressing the impact of orbital-phonon coupling on low-energy excitations.

We investigate the quantum statistical mechanics of laser-cooled atoms within optical lattices that involve dissipative processes. By formulating a formally exact quantum master equation, we demonstrate that these dissipationary mechanisms can induce anomalies in the atoms' thermodynamic behavior. Specifically, we identify non-monotonic relationships between entropy and temperature, as well as negative signatures in specific heat at constant volume. Furthermore, we analyze the origins of these dissipation-driven anomalies by comparing them to results from a purely unitary evolution model simulated using a Projected Gross-Pitaevskii equation (PGPE). These findings reveal that while a PGPE-based effective temperature generally captures the anomalies through its monotonic entropy-temperature dependence, the anomalies in the dilute regime originate instead from modifications to the system's Hamiltonian caused by dissipation.

This study investigates information flow within cryptocurrency markets by constructing a dynamic trading network based on pair-coherence. We split our analysis into two phases: first, we rank cryptocurrencies by trading volume and select only those exceeding specific thresholds to form our research group. Second, we evaluate network dependencies using both pairwise correlations and mutual information, as well as higher-order interactions. Results indicate that these dependency structures vary significantly, exhibiting distinct characteristics in terms of network topology and temporal evolution. While pre-market hours show stronger negative correlations, post-market periods feature weaker correlations with broader network scales. Notably, pre-market information propagation follows a more regular distribution compared to the more diffused pattern observed after the market opens. Crucially, pre-market trading acts as a primary source of information, triggering information "bursts" in the network. Furthermore, we observed a more intricate, higher-order connectivity pattern during pre-market sessions. These interactions extend well beyond simple linear correlations, suggesting that markets operate with greater complexity and that information dissemination among cryptocurrencies involves more extensive joint dependencies before trading resumes.

Formed from trace atmospheric gases, particle nucleation serves as a crucial source of cloud condensation nuclei. While acid-base interactions within H₂SO₄-H₂O clusters are vital for this process, previous *ab initio* molecular dynamics simulations neglected zero-point motion (ZPM). This study incorporates ZPM via ab initio path-integral molecular dynamics to evaluate its significance. We analyzed 225 nanokelvin-temperature simulations of three distinct dimer systems: H₂SO₄-(H₂O)₂, (H₂O)₂-H₂SO₄, and -(H₂O)₂-H₂SO₄ dimers. The results indicate a dramatic reduction in hydrogen bond counts upon including ZPM across all configurations. Specifically, ZPM breaks the internal hydrogen bond within the water dimers, prevents the formation of an H₂SO₄ hydrogen bond, and adds one additional hydrogen bond to the (H₂O)₂-H₂SO₄ assembly. These findings demonstrate that ZPM enhances the exposure of H₂SO₄'s hydrogen bonding sites to surrounding water molecules, a effect significant enough to influence the accuracy of atmospheric nucleation rate predictions.

We introduce the concept of a perception pair $(X,A;\mathcal{P},\mathcal{S})$, consisting of compact Hausdorff spaces where one is a closed subspace of the other, alongside two families of continuous maps—one from $X$ and one from $A$ into Tychonoff spaces $Y$ and $B$, respectively, subject to specific compatibility constraints. Our primary achievement is a theorem demonstrating that the collection of all $\mathcal{P}$-non-expansive operators from $X$ to any locally convex topological vector space $L$, which preserve $\mathcal{P}$-equivalence on $A$ (denoted $\mathcal{P}$-boundedness), forms a compact space equipped with pointwise convergence. This result parallels the Conley-Freedman compactification theorem for bounded operators but applies specifically to these induced perception pairs. Furthermore, we extend this space of $\mathcal{P}$-bounded operators by introducing an introduction into new types of "unrestricted" or "free" variations, yielding further applications in our main findings. We also explore how these perceptions induce families of equivalent operators relative to other continuity requirements, thereby producing important structural theorems. Finally, we examine how our results relate to existing theories involving compactification of function spaces and operators, providing proofs of our claims along with multiple illustrative examples throughout.

Simpler models are often favored over more complex ones, a principle shared by most regularization methods that impose penalties on solution complexity. A common assumption is that this occurs because those mechanisms directly punish complexity; however, our findings for discrete combinatorial optimizers reveal otherwise. We demonstrate that for a broad class of combinatorial problems, regularization terms penalizing anything but the intrinsic property of complexity fail to produce a preference for minimal complexity solutions. Conversely, our results for real-valued functions indicate a-principally, any penalty on the **topological many-to-oneness** (mapping from input to output) effectively induces a bias toward simpler models, regardless of the specific function loss employed. We validate this theory using the explicit **Morse-Cascade loss**, which accurately predicts both solution complexity and training dynamics, thereby supporting the use of simple models as a **model selection criterion** for combinatorial tasks and offering new perspectives for continuous-valued problems.

The paper proposes a technique for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ transitions by employing binned maximum likelihood fits on differential distributions of $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays. This approach offers distinct advantages over the standard method of performing fits on individual Wilson coefficients sequentially. The proposed strategy is validated using Monte Carlo simulations and by analyzing real data from the LHCb dataset ($3\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ collected in 2015 and $1\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ in 2016).

Automated essay scoring stands as a pivotal challenge in Natural Language Processing. As Neural Machine Translation systems have evolved, they have become a preferred framework for addressing this issue, yielding substantial improvements in performance. This paper introduces a strategy for enhancing the automated grading of compositions through data augmentation. We focus on translating original answers into their corresponding essays to create new training instances for Neural Machine Translation models. These data points are generated using a Seq2Seq transformer trained and fine-tuned on the Commonsense Knowledge data set. We demonstrate that this approach increases the accuracy of the Neural Machine Translation models employed for scoring, a conclusion supported by experiments on the IMC 2018 contest dataset.

We define marginal independence models based on a given set of random variables, where each marginal distribution must belong to a pre-specified family. We demonstrate that these models form a polytope characterizable through system of linear inequalities, with solutions that compute their dimension and verify membership. Moreover, we establish that the computation of the number of positive real roots for a single-variable polynomial equation with coefficients in a commutative ring is algorithmic within a discrete logarithmic depth neural network context, implying a connection to neural computation limits.

We introduce a dynamic framework for vertical mobility featuring finite time horizons that vary according to a two-point distribution. Under specific conditions, we establish existence and uniqueness solutions for this dynamic program, which can be seen as a quasi-variational inequality, and demonstrate the smoothness of the value function. Additionally, we analyze the asymptotic behavior as time horizons extend to ensure that unique solutions exist uniformly across the limit to a deterministic, continuous time model. Finally, we examine a allocation puzzle arising from varying time horizon lengths: when efforts are imperfectly transmitted across generations, higher potential individuals are granted more opportunities; however, if efforts are perfectly determined by parental inputs, those with lower potential receive more opportunities.

Hebrew Natural Language Processing (HLP) has experienced significant expansion recently, marked by notable strides in machine translation, semantic parsing, and other core areas. A primary catalyst for this growth is the Second Wave of Hebrew Treebanks, which introduces new data for tokenization, lemmatization, constituency parsing, and various other linguistic analyses. This article specifically addresses treebanking efforts and presents insights into creating a Hebreu Treebank. It also evaluates cross-domain parsing capabilities, comparing state-of-the-art parsers against each other and the domain of the training data.

Driven by machine learning's rising influence on model-assisted scientific decision-making, achieving enhanced accuracy and reliability is becoming paramount. We introduce "Cooperative Data-Driven Modeling" (CDDM), a novel ensemble strategy designed to refine black-box mathematical representations of complex physical systems. The approach involves partitioning training data into local subsets to generate individual constituent models, which are subsequently refined through an inductive transfer step that shares white-box structural metadata—such as equation topology and parameter constraints—among them while preserving their black-box functional flexibility. This structural collaboration enables CDDM to function as a highly adaptable structural ensemble. Preliminary tests on real-world urban traffic forecasting and synthetic fluid dynamics problems reveal that CDDM surpasses both random and iterative ensemble methods in accuracy.

Low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes constitute a prominent class of linear block error-correcting codes defined by their sparse parity-check matrices. Representing these structures as bipartite graphs, where one vertex type corresponds to message bits and the other to parity constraints, reveals a degree distribution that significantly influences decoding performance. To address this, the degree-degree correlation (DDC) coefficient offers a novel metric designed to quantify the link between the input and output degree degrees within this bipartite framework. This study investigates how the DDC coefficient affects the performance of finite-length LDPC codes when transmitted through a binary erasure channel (BEC). Specifically, the work derives a formula for calculating vertex degree degrees based on average values and bounds the co-efficient's range. Furthermore, the research establishes a relationship between DCC, vertex average degrees, and sparsity. Numerical evaluations support these findings.

The predictive safety filter (PSF) recently introduced in literature has gained attention for its ability to guarantee system stability while ensuring safety by predicting system behavior. Although highly effective, the traditional PSF suffers from significant computational complexity, making real-time implementation impractical for systems of any scale. To overcome this barrier, this study proposes implementing system-level synthesis within a model predictive control (MLC) framework specifically tailored for structured systems. By leveraging structural properties to drastically reduce computational demands, this new approach preserves the safety guarantees provided by the original PSF while offering lower complexity. The formulation and analysis of the proposed method are demonstrated on a system exhibiting rotational symmetry as well as through safety-critical verification in a wind turbine generator system, where performance is compared against standard MLC approaches.

Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) enables two parties to create a shared, truly random secret key, secured by the fundamental laws of quantum mechanics, even if one does not have access to them. While real-world QKD implementations are vulnerable to side channels—such as imperfections in practical light sources that allow eavesdroppers to exploit attack vectors unlike those possible with ideal devices—the "heralding side-channel attack" specifically targets non-randomized phases in the signal states. In this work, we investigate a variant where the eavesdropper performs hardware manipulation on only a subset of the phases within the emitted pulses. Our analysis reveals this vector remains undetectable through standard quantum security verification. However, our results also demonstrate that such an attack functions only if the receiver's measurement basis is biased toward specific angles; this creates a mitigation strategy by advising users to randomly distribute their detection angles, thereby rendering such an attack viable only under very limited conditions from the attacker's perspective. Consequently, when combined with proper system-level randomness controls, similar physical-layer hacks are rendered impractical for the attacker.

Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive capabilities across diverse tasks through in-context few-shot learning. This study examines how different pretraining corpora affect such learning. Specifically, it investigates varied dataset compositions used to train 7B and 13B parameter models, assessing their in-context performance on eight benchmarks. The results indicate that broad, general corpora do not necessarily outperform narrow ones; in many cases, limited-corpus models exhibit superior or equal efficacy. Furthermore, analyzing the large-scale corpus's impact reveals that even when these datasets are enriched with task-specific data post-training, the model's few-shot effectiveness remains unchanged. Ultimately, the author argues that few-shot performance depends less on the breadth of pretraining data and more on the quality and focus of added supplementary materials.

While radiative cooling drives the formation of a cooling flow within the central regions of galaxy clusters, this process is fundamentally altered by gravitational instability, which triggers the collapse of cooling gas into central cold clouds. These clouds subsequently disintegrate, influencing the group's overall dynamics. Although the mechanisms behind cloud proliferation and expansion remain an active area of study, this study demonstrates that both growth and the division of these clouds can effectively halt cooling. We examine the evolution of a single cold cloud over a span of 100 Myears using high-resolution simulations to analyze how magnetic fields, thermal conduction, and initial cloud parameters dictate their behavior. Results indicate that cloud size and magnetic field strength primarily dictate whether a cloud expands or fragments, whereas thermal conination predominantly dictates expansion rates. Specifically, strong magnetic fields favor cloud expansion, while turbulent adiabatic compression tends to increase cloud numbers. Moreover, cloud expansion rates are significantly faster than their expansion velocities, a critical distinction for understanding feedback loops. Finally, our findings suggest that cloud expansion and subsequent fragmentation offer a more efficient energy feedback mechanism compared to simple heating, as they act over a broader spatial and temporal scale.

Future mobile networks will increasingly rely on automation to cut operational expenses, a shift central to the concept of Self-Organizing Networks (SON) underpinning 5G architectures. Our goal is to identify strategic improvements that ensure CNM can effectively sustain future, self-sustaining, and sustainable mobile networks.

Motion planning is a fundamental challenge in robotics, robotics, and control theory. We introduce a data-driven method for constructing multi-stage coupled convex optimizations designed to plan robot motion. Each optimization stage represents a specific time window, and we apply McCormick envelope relaxations to the kinematic constraints to ensure computational tractability. This approach allows for rapid solve times while maintaining sufficient accuracy for practical applications. Furthermore, each stage is a differential inclusion that approximates a individual optimal control problem, enabling the method to function as both a planning tool and a real-time controller capable of reacting to dynamic environmental changes. This study explores the motion of a walking coffee cup through a simplified single-degree-of-freedom pendulum model. The analysis focuses on how the driving parameters of this oscillation are influenced by the cup's sloshing dynamics. Results indicate that for cup fill levels exceeding 20%, stable limit cycles emerge, enabling perpetual oscillation. This paper introduces a distributionally robust learning algorithm designed to address cases where data sampling distributions are subject to significant uncertainty. Leveraging the robust optimization framework, we formulate a convex minimax problem that minimizes risk by its worst-case distribution within an ambiguity set defined by the Wasserstein metric based on empirical data. By combining the augmented Lagrangian method with the conditional gradient method, we derive a sampling algorithm capable of distributing learning across a network in a fully decentralized manner, ensuring privacy by requiring communication only between adjacent nodes. Under standard assumptions, we prove the convergence of this DR-DSGD approach to the optimal minimax solution and establish a communication complexity order for reaching an $\varepsilon$-approximate stationary point. Additionally, we demonstrate an $\varepsilon$-approximate solution can be reached with finite samples from any arbitrary initial distribution, with total communication rounds being the primary sample-dependent factor.
